field_changes.after: Church land was being inventoried in preparation for sale while monasteries and convents were closing.

field_changes.before: Initially cooperative clergy confronted cumulative loss of revenues, feudal rights, property and autonomy. Utility-based suppression closed most monasteries and convents while retaining functional exceptions and prohibiting new binding vows. State dependence raised minimum salaries for some priests but brought cuts or uncertain payment for others; inventories and sales turned reform into local loyalty tests. Clerical deputies initially helped transform the Estates-General while expecting reform, not destruction of the clergy’s corporate status or autonomy. The abolition of tithes, dues, pluralism, and papal payments, followed by nationalization of Church property, removed the clergy’s independent material base and made it dependent on state salaries. The Assembly dissolved most regular religious houses and prohibited new vows, retaining only institutions serving education or charity. The nation seized ecclesiastical estates, inventoried them, and prepared their sale while taking responsibility for charitable and educational functions. After taking ecclesiastical property, the nation promised salaries to clergy and assumed responsibility for education and charity, making the Church materially dependent on the state.
